meta.titre: Polar Coordinates: Curves, Areas and Motion in Radial and Transverse Components

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Further Mathematics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A radar operator at Douala airport locates an aircraft by its distance from the antenna and the bearing of the line of sight, not by east-west and north-south distances. The rotating sprinkler on a rice field in Ndop and the spiral of a mosquito coil are described the same way. Polar coordinates suit every situation where the distance from a fixed point and the direction around it matter more than a square grid. In GCE Further Mathematics you must convert between the two systems, recognise the standard curves, find areas, and split the motion of a particle into radial and transverse parts.

items: In a right-angled triangle, $\cos\theta$ is adjacent over hypotenuse and $\sin\theta$ is opposite over hypotenuse.
The identities $\cos^2\theta=\tfrac12(1+\cos2\theta)$ and $\sin^2\theta=\tfrac12(1-\cos2\theta)$ hold for every angle.
Angles in calculus are measured in radians, and a definite integral gives an accumulated area.
The chain rule gives $\dfrac{dr}{dt}=\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\,\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}$ for a function $r(\theta)$.

sections.titre: From (x, y) to (r, theta): conversion, standard curves, area and motion
sections.contenu_markdown:
A point $P$ is fixed by $(r,\theta)$: $r$ is its distance from the **pole** $O$, and $\theta$ is the angle from the **initial line** (the positive $x$-axis) measured anticlockwise to $OP$. The two systems are linked by

$$
x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta \tag{1}
$$

$$
r^2=x^2+y^2,\qquad \tan\theta=\frac{y}{x} \tag{2}
$$

In (2) the calculator returns an angle in the first or fourth quadrant only, so always decide the quadrant of $\theta$ from the signs of $x$ and $y$.

| Polar equation | Curve |
|---|---|
| $r=a$ | circle, centre $O$, radius $a$ |
| $\theta=\alpha$ | straight line through $O$ |
| $r=2a\cos\theta$ | circle through $O$, centre $(a,0)$, radius $a$ |
| $r=2a\sin\theta$ | circle through $O$, centre $(0,a)$, radius $a$ |
| $r=a(1+\cos\theta)$ | cardioid, symmetric about the initial line |
| $r^2=a^2\cos2\theta$ | lemniscate (figure of eight), loops along the initial line |

To sketch a curve, test symmetry (replacing $\theta$ by $-\theta$ gives symmetry in the initial line), find where $r=0$ (the tangent at the pole is then the line $\theta=\theta_0$, where $\theta_0$ is that angle), find the greatest $r$, and remember that a point with $r<0$ is plotted on the opposite side of the pole, in the direction $\theta+\pi$.

variantes.nom: Converting equations between the two systems
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a curve is given in one system and the question or a calculation is easier in the other.
variantes.contenu_markdown: To go from Cartesian to polar, replace $x$ and $y$ using (1), simplify, and divide by $r$ only if the pole is still on the curve. For example $x^2+y^2=6x$ becomes $r^2=6r\cos\theta$, so $r=6\cos\theta$ (the pole is on this curve at $\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, so nothing is lost). To go from polar to Cartesian, multiply by $r$ so that the pieces $r\cos\theta=x$, $r\sin\theta=y$ and $r^2=x^2+y^2$ appear. For example $r=6\sin\theta$ gives $r^2=6r\sin\theta$, that is $x^2+y^2=6y$. Remember $\sin\theta=\dfrac{y}{r}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{x}{r}$.

variantes.nom: Area enclosed by a polar curve
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the area of a region bounded by a polar curve and two radial lines, or between two polar curves, is required.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
The area swept by the radius from $\theta=\alpha$ to $\theta=\beta$ is

$$
A=\frac12\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} r^{2}\,d\theta \tag{3}
$$

provided $r\ge0$ and the curve is traced once as $\theta$ goes from $\alpha$ to $\beta$. Use symmetry to halve the work. For a region between an inner curve $r_1$ and an outer curve $r_2$ the area is $\tfrac12\int(r_2^{2}-r_1^{2})\,d\theta$. When two curves cross, find the intersection angles by equating the two values of $r$, then decide for each range of $\theta$ which curve is nearer the pole.

variantes.nom: Radial and transverse components of velocity and acceleration
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a particle moves on a curve given in polar form and the question asks for the radial or transverse part of its velocity or acceleration.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Write $\dot r=\dfrac{dr}{dt}$ and $\dot\theta=\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}$. Along the radius and perpendicular to it (the direction of increasing $\theta$):

$$
v_r=\dot r,\qquad v_\theta=r\dot\theta \tag{4}
$$

$$
a_r=\ddot r-r\dot\theta^{2},\qquad a_\theta=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta=\frac1r\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(r^{2}\dot\theta\bigr) \tag{5}
$$

The speed satisfies $v^2=\dot r^{2}+r^{2}\dot\theta^{2}$. When $\dot\theta=\omega$ is constant, $\ddot\theta=0$, so $a_\theta=2\dot r\omega$, and $\dot r=\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\,\omega$ by the chain rule.

sections.enonce_markdown: The circle $C_1$ has polar equation $r=4\cos\theta$ and the circle $C_2$ has polar equation $r=2$. Find the exact area of the region lying inside both circles.

etapes.justification: Converting $C_1$ to Cartesian form shows its centre and radius, which tells us which angles the region occupies.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Multiplying by $r$: $r^2=4r\cos\theta$, so $x^2+y^2=4x$, that is $(x-2)^2+y^2=4$. $C_1$ has centre $(2,0)$ and radius $2$; $C_2$ has centre $O$ and radius $2$. $C_1$ lies in the half-plane $x\ge0$, so only $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ is needed.

etapes.justification: Equating the two values of $r$ gives the angles at which the boundary changes from one curve to the other.

etapes.action: Decide which curve bounds the region for each range of $\theta$.
etapes.justification: A ray from the pole leaves the common region at the nearer of the two curves, that is at the smaller value of $r$.
etapes.resultat_markdown: For $-\tfrac{\pi}{3}\le\theta\le\tfrac{\pi}{3}$, $4\cos\theta\ge2$, so the boundary is $r=2$. For $\tfrac{\pi}{3}\le\theta\le\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $4\cos\theta\le2$, so the boundary is $r=4\cos\theta$. The region is symmetric about the initial line.

etapes.action: Write the area with formula (3) and use symmetry.
etapes.justification: Double the upper half, splitting it at $\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{3}$.

etapes.action: Evaluate, using $\cos^2\theta=\tfrac12(1+\cos2\theta)$ in the second integral.
etapes.justification: The first integral is a constant; the second needs the double-angle form.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The area is $\dfrac{8\pi}{3}-2\sqrt3\approx4.91$ square units. This is sensible: it is smaller than the area $4\pi\approx12.6$ of either circle.

items.erreur_markdown: Converting the point $(-3,3)$ to polar form as $r=3\sqrt2$, $\theta=\arctan(-1)=-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The calculator gives an angle in the fourth quadrant, but $(-3,3)$ is in the second quadrant ($x<0$, $y>0$). The point $(3\sqrt2,-\tfrac{\pi}{4})$ is $(3,-3)$.
items.correction_markdown: Decide the quadrant first: $\theta=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$. Check: $3\sqrt2\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=-3$ and $3\sqrt2\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=3$.

items.erreur_markdown: Finding the area of the circle $r=2\cos\theta$ as $\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta=2\pi$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The factor $\tfrac12$ in $A=\tfrac12\int r^2\,d\theta$ was forgotten. The circle has radius $1$, so its area cannot be $2\pi$.

items.erreur_markdown: Integrating $\tfrac12\int r^2\,d\theta$ for the circle $r=2\cos\theta$ from $\theta=0$ to $\theta=2\pi$ because a full turn is $2\pi$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The circle $r=2\cos\theta$ is traced once while $\theta$ runs through an interval of length $\pi$, from $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ to $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. Over $0$ to $2\pi$ it is traced twice, so the area is doubled and the result is $2\pi$.
items.correction_markdown: Integrate over one tracing only, for example $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, to get $\pi$.

items.erreur_markdown: Stating that the radial acceleration of a particle moving on the circle $r=3$ with constant angular speed $\omega=2$ is $\ddot r=0$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The unit vector along the radius itself turns with the particle. This produces the extra term $-r\dot\theta^{2}$, which is the acceleration directed towards the pole.
items.correction_markdown: $a_r=\ddot r-r\dot\theta^{2}=0-3(2)^2=-12$, a magnitude of $12$ directed towards the pole.

items.erreur_markdown: Converting $r=6\sin\theta$ to Cartesian form by writing $\sin\theta=\dfrac{y}{x}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The ratio $\dfrac{y}{x}$ is $\tan\theta$. In the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $r$, $\sin\theta=\dfrac{y}{r}$.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Express the point with Cartesian coordinates $(-2,-2\sqrt3)$ in polar form $(r,\theta)$ with $r>0$ and $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. (b) Find a Cartesian equation of the curve $r=8\cos\theta$ and state its centre and radius.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $r=\sqrt{4+12}=4$. The point is in the third quadrant, and $\tan\theta=\dfrac{-2\sqrt3}{-2}=\sqrt3$, whose first-quadrant angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. In the third quadrant, with $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$, $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\pi=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. The polar form is **$\left(4,-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$**. Check: $4\cos(-\tfrac{2\pi}{3})=-2$ and $4\sin(-\tfrac{2\pi}{3})=-2\sqrt3$.

(b) Multiply by $r$: $r^2=8r\cos\theta$, so $x^2+y^2=8x$, that is **$(x-4)^2+y^2=16$**: a circle with centre $(4,0)$ and radius $4$.

items.enonce_markdown: The curve $L$ has Cartesian equation $(x^2+y^2)^2=9(x^2-y^2)$. (a) Show that its polar equation can be written $r^2=9\cos2\theta$. (b) Find the area enclosed by the loop of $L$ that lies along the positive $x$-axis.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Substitute $x^2+y^2=r^2$ and $x^2-y^2=r^2\cos^2\theta-r^2\sin^2\theta=r^2\cos2\theta$: $r^4=9r^2\cos2\theta$. Dividing by $r^2$ is allowed because the pole lies on $r^2=9\cos2\theta$ (take $\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{4}$), so **$r^2=9\cos2\theta$**.

(b) For the right-hand loop $r$ is real when $\cos2\theta\ge0$, that is $-\tfrac{\pi}{4}\le\theta\le\tfrac{\pi}{4}$. Then $A=\tfrac12\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}9\cos2\theta\,d\theta=\tfrac92\left[\dfrac{\sin2\theta}{2}\right]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}=\tfrac92\left(\tfrac12+\tfrac12\right)=$ **$\dfrac92$ square units**.

items.enonce_markdown: A particle $P$ moves on the circle with polar equation $r=2a\cos\theta$ ($a>0$) so that $\dot\theta=\omega$, a constant. (a) Find the radial and transverse components of the velocity of $P$ and show that its speed is constant. (b) Find the radial and transverse components of its acceleration and show that the magnitude of the acceleration is $4a\omega^2$.
items.solution_markdown:
With $\dot\theta=\omega$ and $\ddot\theta=0$: $\dot r=\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\omega=-2a\omega\sin\theta$ and $\ddot r=-2a\omega\cdot\omega\cos\theta=-2a\omega^2\cos\theta$.

(a) $v_r=\dot r=$ **$-2a\omega\sin\theta$** and $v_\theta=r\dot\theta=$ **$2a\omega\cos\theta$**. Speed: $v^2=4a^2\omega^2\sin^2\theta+4a^2\omega^2\cos^2\theta=4a^2\omega^2$, so $v=2a\omega$, a constant.

(b) $a_r=\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2=-2a\omega^2\cos\theta-2a\cos\theta\,\omega^2=$ **$-4a\omega^2\cos\theta$**, and $a_\theta=2\dot r\omega=$ **$-4a\omega^2\sin\theta$** (since $\ddot\theta=0$). The magnitude is $\sqrt{16a^2\omega^4\cos^2\theta+16a^2\omega^4\sin^2\theta}=4a\omega^2$. This agrees with motion on a circle of radius $a$ at speed $2a\omega$, where $\dfrac{v^2}{a}=4a\omega^2$.

items_markdown: $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$, $r^2=x^2+y^2$, $\tan\theta=y/x$; choose the quadrant of $\theta$ from the signs of $x$ and $y$.
To convert an equation, multiply or divide by $r$ so that $r\cos\theta$, $r\sin\theta$ and $r^2$ appear, and remember $\sin\theta=y/r$.
Standard curves: $r=a$ (circle), $\theta=\alpha$ (line through the pole), $r=2a\cos\theta$ (circle through the pole), $r=a(1+\cos\theta)$ (cardioid), $r^2=a^2\cos2\theta$ (lemniscate).
Area: $A=\tfrac12\int_\alpha^\beta r^2\,d\theta$. Integrate over one tracing of the curve and use symmetry; for two curves, compare $r$ in each range of $\theta$.
